Apply Lucas's theorem with p = 2 to determine parity of C(n, k)

conclude zeros = v5(P) = 1124

Endpoint Product as Perfect Square Const.name: Endpoint Product as Perfect Square Constraint
Endpoint Product as Perfect Square Const.description: The product of the first and last digits (a c) must be a perfect square; enumerate possible endpoint pairs by testing squares up to 9*9.
cues: a ≠ c
ac must be a perfect square (t ∈ {1,4,9,16,25,36,49,64,81})
implementation: For each t in {1,4,9,16,25,36,49,64,81}, consider b = sqrt(t) (integer 1..9)
List factor pairs (a, c) with a c = t and a, c ∈ {1,...,9}, a ≠ c
Form numbers by placing b in the middle: abc

GCD–LCM Decomposition.name: GCD–LCM Decomposition
GCD–LCM Decomposition.description: Use x = g s and y = g t with gcd(s,t) = 1 and L = g s t to separate common and coprime prime content and rewrite equations in terms of g,s,t.
cues: gcd(x,y) = g and lcm(x,y) = L appear in the setup
x = g s, y = g t with gcd(s,t) = 1
implementation: derive x g^2 = 10^60 and y L^2 = 10^570 from the log equations
use L = g s t to obtain y L^2 = g^3 s^2 t^3 = 10^570
divide second equation by the first to get s t^3 = 10^510

Log-space Linearization.name: Log-space Linearization
Log-space Linearization.description: Replace variables by their base-10 logarithms to convert multiplicative relations into linear equations.
cues: define A = log10 g, S = log10 s, T = log10 t
yield linear equations: S + 3A = 60 and 3A + 2S + 3T = 570
implementation: from S + 3A = 60 deduce S = 60 − 3A
substitute into 3A + 2S + 3T = 570 to get T = A + 150

Coprime Exponent Constraint.name: Coprime Exponent Constraint
Coprime Exponent Constraint.description: Use gcd(s,t) = 1 to force non-overlapping prime exponents between s and t, solving for exponents via prime-factor decomposition of the equations.
cues: analyze prime 2 and prime 5 exponents: s2 = 60 − 3a2, t2 = a2 + 150; s5 = 60 − 3a5, t5 = a5 + 150
gcd(s,t) = 1 implies min(s2,t2) = 0 and min(s5,t5) = 0
implementation: since t2 ≥ 150, deduce s2 = 0 → a2 = 20 and t2 = 170
since t5 ≥ 150, deduce s5 = 0 → a5 = 20 and t5 = 170

Prime-power Factorization and Multiplici.name: Prime-power Factorization and Multiplicity Count
Prime-power Factorization and Multiplici.description: After reconstructing x and y, count total prime factors with multiplicity to compute m and n, then form the required linear combination.
implementation: m = total prime factors in x = 20 + 20 = 40
n = total prime factors in y = 190 + 190 = 380

Farey Neighbor Mediant Rule.name: Farey Neighbor Mediant Rule
Farey Neighbor Mediant Rule.description: If a/b < c/d with bc − ad = 1, then a/b and c/d are consecutive in some Farey sequence; the mediant (a+c)/(b+d) lies strictly between them and has the smallest possible denominator among all fractions between.
cues: bc − ad = 1
a/b and c/d are in lowest terms
there exists a fraction strictly between them
implementation: identify the mediant (a+c)/(b+d) = (5+4)/(9+7) = 9/16 as between 5/9 and 4/7
note the denominator is b+d = 16, which is minimal among fractions strictly between them

Mediant Minimizes Denominator Between Fa.name: Mediant Minimizes Denominator Between Farey Neighbors
Mediant Minimizes Denominator Between Fa.description: Among all fractions strictly between two Farey neighbors, the mediant has the minimal possible denominator.
cues: bc − ad = 1 for the two fractions
mediant provides a between-frac with smallest denominator
implementation: compute mediant to obtain p/q = 9/16 with q = 16
conclude q − p = 7

Fractional-Plus-Constant Decomposition.name: Fractional-Plus-Constant Decomposition

parameters.name: coefficients
parameters.description: (p, q) such that (p a + q b)/(a + b) = k + m · a/(a+b)

Fractional-Plus-Constant Decomposition.description: Rewrite a rational expression of the form (p a + q b)/(a + b) as a constant plus a multiple of a/(a+b) to separate a fixed part from a positive fractional part.
cues: expression (81a + 16b)/(a + b) appears after factoring out common powers
a, b > 0 allows writing as 16 + 65 a/(a+b)
implementation: factor the numerator: 81a + 16b = 16(a + b) + 65a
obtain the decomposition: (81a + 16b)/(a+b) = 16 + 65 a/(a+b)

Exponential Ratio Bounding via Root Comp.name: Exponential Ratio Bounding via Root Comparison
Exponential Ratio Bounding via Root Comp.description: Bound a ratio of large powers by expressing it as a simple power ratio and then comparing via an inequality on the bases.
cues: rewrite as (81/16)^24 to facilitate comparison
target threshold 64 corresponds to 64 = 2^6 and its 24th root is 2^{1/4}
implementation: compare with 64 via taking 24th roots: 64^{1/24} = 2^{1/4}
since 81/16 > 2^{1/4}, conclude a/b > 64 and hence a > 64 b

Floor Bounding via Narrow Interval.name: Floor Bounding via Narrow Interval
Floor Bounding via Narrow Interval.description: Determine the floor of a quantity by proving it lies strictly between two consecutive integers.
cues: after decomposition, the quantity equals 16 + 65a/(a+b)
since a/(a+b) ∈ (0,1), the expression lies in (16, 81)
specifically show it is > 80 and < 81 to deduce floor = 80
implementation: show a > 64 b implies 16 + 65 a/(a+b) > 80
also use a/(a+b) < 1 to deduce 16 + 65 a/(a+b) < 81

Decimal Concatenation as Base-10 Polynom.name: Decimal Concatenation as Base-10 Polynomial

parameters.name: sequence
parameters.description: the sequence of integers being concatenated (here 1..44)

Decimal Concatenation as Base-10 Polynom.description: Interpret the concatenation of integers as evaluating a base-10 polynomial where each digit occupies a place value.
cues: problem constructs N by concatenating 1 through 44
the value of N depends on place-values of digits in base 10
implementation: model N as sum of its digits times powers of 10, i.e., N = d_0 + d_1·10 + d_2·10^2 + ... with digits taken in order from 1 to 44

Last-Digit Modulo 5.name: Last-Digit Modulo 5
Last-Digit Modulo 5.description: The remainder modulo 5 is determined by the final decimal digit of a number.
cues: last digit of N is the last digit of 44, namely 4
implementation: conclude N ≡ 4 (mod 5) from the last digit

Trailing-9s Carry Propagation.name: Trailing-9s Carry Propagation
Trailing-9s Carry Propagation.description: When a number ends with k 9s, adding 1 turns those 9s into 0s and increments the preceding digit; use this to compute how the digit-sum changes.
cues: problem states n has k trailing 9s
incrementing n yields a predictable change in the digit-sum: S(n+1) = S(n) + 1 − 9k
implementation: derive S(n+1) = S(prefix) + (d+1) + 0s − (d + 9k) = S(n) − 9k + 1
hence S(n+1) = S(n) + 1 − 9k

Trailing-9s Feasibility Construction.name: Trailing-9s Feasibility Construction
Trailing-9s Feasibility Construction.description: Provide a constructive example showing feasibility of a given k trailing 9s by choosing a prefix with a suitable sum and appending k trailing 9s
cues: after determining k, demonstrate existence by constructing digits with desired S(n)
implementation: example: prefix summing to 1230, preceding digit 8, and four trailing 9s yields S(n) = 1230 + 8 + 36 = 1274

Tau-Exponent Mapping for Prime Powers.name: Tau-Exponent Mapping for Prime Powers

parameters.name: prime_exponents
parameters.description: mapping of primes to their exponents in n (e.g., a for 2, b for 5, c for 11)

Tau-Exponent Mapping for Prime Powers.description: Use the multiplicative formula tau(n) = ∏(e_i + 1) to translate divisor-count requirements into equations on prime exponents.
cues: tau(110 n^3) is required to equal 110
implementation: compute exponents in 110 n^3: for 2, exponent = 3a+1; for tau factor add 1 -> 3a+2; similarly 3b+2 and 3c+2
express tau(110 n^3) as (3a+2)(3b+2)(3c+2)

Restricted-Prime Set by Tau-Counting.name: Restricted-Prime Set by Tau-Counting
Restricted-Prime Set by Tau-Counting.description: Argue that no new prime factors can appear in n because they would introduce an extra tau-factor that cannot divide the target tau-value.
cues: if n contained p^e with p ≠ 2,5,11, then tau(110 n^3) would gain a factor (3e+1) ≥ 4
110's divisors are {1,2,5,10,11,22,55,110}, none are multiples of 4
implementation: conclude n can involve only primes 2, 5, and 11

Exponent Pattern Matching to Divisor Str.name: Exponent Pattern Matching to Divisor Structure

parameters.name: target_factorization
parameters.description: desired triple of tau-factors (as (e_i+1) values) corresponding to primes in n

Exponent Pattern Matching to Divisor Str.description: After restricting primes, match the tau factors to the prime-count target by comparing to divisors of 110.
cues: divisors of 110 that can be written in the form 3k+2 are 2, 5, 11
implementation: deduce that {3a+2, 3b+2, 3c+2} must be {2,5,11} up to order
hence {a,b,c} = {0,1,3}

Tau-Power Evaluation for Higher Exponent.name: Tau-Power Evaluation for Higher Exponent

parameters.name: fixed_factor_tau
parameters.description: tau-value contributed by the fixed base-power (e.g., tau(81) = 5 for 3^4)

Tau-Power Evaluation for Higher Exponent.description: Compute tau for a higher-power factor when n is fixed, by substituting the exponents into tau-formula and including the tau of the fixed factor.
cues: with {a,b,c} = {0,1,3}, compute tau(81 n^4)
n^4 contributes exponents 4a,4b,4c
implementation: substitute a,b,c to obtain a specific numeric value

3-adic Valuation.name: 3-adic Valuation
3-adic Valuation.description: exponent of 3 in the prime factorization of n; v3(n)
cues: problem partitions numbers by the highest power of 3 dividing n
implementation: write n = 3^a · m with 3 ∤ m, where a = v3(n)

Chains under Multiplication by 3.name: Chains under Multiplication by 3

parameters.name: chain length

Chains under Multiplication by 3.description: partition integers into chains n, 3n, 9n, 27n, ... with ratio 3 between consecutive terms
cues: for fixed m with 3 ∤ m, the subsequence m, 3m, 9m, 27m, 81m, ... forms a chain
implementation: within a chain, you cannot pick two consecutive terms (since one is three times the other)
for a chain of length k+1, the maximum pick is floor(k/2) + 1

Independent Set on Path Graph.name: Independent Set on Path Graph

parameters.name: chain_length
parameters.description: length of the chain (number of terms)

Independent Set on Path Graph.description: maximum independent set in a chain (path graph) is achieved by taking every other node

a constructive choice is to take a even (a = 0, 2, 4, ...) in each chain

Primitive Root Modulo Prime.name: Primitive Root Modulo Prime
Primitive Root Modulo Prime.description: The nonzero residues modulo a prime p form a cyclic group of order p−1; a primitive root is an element of multiplicative order p−1; the number of primitive roots is φ(p−1).
cues: problem works modulo a prime
multiplicative group of units modulo p has order p−1
need an element whose powers cycle through all nonzero residues
implementation: used to determine there are φ(p−1) primitive roots and to identify candidates by order tests

Generate All Primitive Roots from a Know.name: Generate All Primitive Roots from a Known Primitive Root

primitive roots are given by powers with exponents coprime to p−1
for p=7, p−1=6 and coprime exponents are {1,5}
implementation: after confirming 3 is primitive, generate 3^1 and 3^5 to obtain all primitive roots (3 and 5)

Order of an Element mod p (Multiplicativ.name: Order of an Element mod p (Multiplicative Order)
Order of an Element mod p (Multiplicativ.description: The order of a modulo p is the smallest positive t with a^t ≡ 1 (mod p); for a ≠ 0 mod p, the order divides p−1.
cues: order divides p−1
verifying whether 3 has full order by checking powers
implementation: used to test that 3 has order 6 (the full p−1 for p=7) by inspecting the cycle lengths: 3^6 ≡ 1 and no smaller exponent yields 1

Discriminant as Perfect Square.name: Discriminant as Perfect Square
Discriminant as Perfect Square.description: For a quadratic with integer coefficients, the roots are rational iff the discriminant is a nonnegative perfect square.
cues: problem uses discriminant to determine rationality of roots
coefficients are a = 2, b = 5, c = b (variable parameter)
discriminant Δ = b^2 − 4ac = 25 − 8b must be a nonnegative square
implementation: set Δ = t^2 with t ∈ Z≥0, so 25 − 8b = t^2
rearrange to 8b = 25 − t^2, hence b = (25 − t^2)/8
require b to be a positive integer; test t such that t^2 ≤ 25

Discriminant-Based Parameter Elimination.name: Discriminant-Based Parameter Elimination

parameters.name: t

Discriminant-Based Parameter Elimination.description: Solve for parameter values by turning the discriminant condition into a simple diophantine equation and testing feasible integer solutions.
cues: Δ must be nonnegative
b must be a positive integer
only small t yield integer b
implementation: substitute Δ = t^2 into 25 − 8b = t^2, giving 8b = 25 − t^2
since b > 0, require 0 ≤ t^2 ≤ 25; consider t ∈ {0,1,2,3,4,5}
identify t values yielding integer b: t = 1 gives b = 3; t = 3 gives b = 2
sum of feasible b values = 5

GCD Denominator Reduction.name: GCD Denominator Reduction
GCD Denominator Reduction.description: Use gcd(n, m) to reduce a fraction to lowest terms by canceling common factors with the denominator; the resulting denominator reveals the remaining prime factors to check.
cues: the fraction n/120 is reduced by gcd(n,120) to n/(120)
the termination criterion depends on the reduced denominator's prime factors

analyze prime factors of 120/d; to terminate, 120/d must have only 2 and 5 as primes
observe 120/d has a potential factor 3 unless d contains the 3; hence 3 | n
conclude that n must be a multiple of 3; number of such n in 1..120 is floor(120/3) = 40

Carry-Driven Alphametic Solver.name: Carry-Driven Alphametic Solver

digits S, E, B, A are distinct and nonzero as leading letters

use hundreds and thousands columns to derive a second expression for A and a relation involving c3

Modular Constraint from Column Sums.name: Modular Constraint from Column Sums
Modular Constraint from Column Sums.description: Translate column-sum equations into modular constraints to bound carries and relate digits, exploiting 0 ≤ digits < base.

Consistency via Two A-Expressions.description: When a single digit A appears in two different linear expressions, equate them to derive a solvable relation among other variables.

A must satisfy A = 3E + 2 − b*c3 (from hundreds column)

solve for b in terms of E and c3: b = (4E + 3 + c3) / (1 + c3)
test feasible c3 values (noting c3 ∈ {1,2} due to distinctness of digits and no overflow)

Block-wise Period Counting (mod 9).name: Block-wise Period Counting (mod 9)
Block-wise Period Counting (mod 9).description: Break the integers into blocks of length 9 and count how many satisfy a fixed residue condition within each block; then locate the nth satisfied value by block and offset.

each 9-block contains a fixed number of valid residues

thus 5 valid numbers per block; the 22nd valid number lies in block 4 with offset 2, giving 38

Denominator Determination by gcd with 99.description: The reduced denominator equals 99 / gcd(99, N); possible denominators come from divisors of 99, excluding the impossible gcd when N = 0 or N = 99.

symmetry about the y-axis; x-values are integers from -2 to 2

Example counts: x=−2 or 2 → 1 point; x=−1 or 1 → 5 points; x=0 → 7 points

Divisibility by 6 for product of three c.name: Divisibility by 6 for product of three consecutive integers
Divisibility by 6 for product of three c.description: The product of any three consecutive integers is always divisible by 6 because it contains a multiple of 2 and a multiple of 3.

Among any three consecutive integers, one is even and one is multiple of 3

Common divisor bound via gcd of a finite.name: Common divisor bound via gcd of a finite sample
Common divisor bound via gcd of a finite.description: To bound a universal common divisor for all composite-n values of f(n), compute the gcd of f on a small finite set of composite n; any common divisor must divide that gcd.

Inclusion-Exclusion for Square Divisors.name: Inclusion-Exclusion for Square Divisors
Inclusion-Exclusion for Square Divisors.description: Count numbers up to a limit that are divisible by at least one prime square by adding singles and subtracting overlaps using LCMs.
cues: problem asks for count of numbers ≤ N divisible by 4, 9, 25, or 49
overlaps must be accounted for via common multiples (LCMs)
implementation: compute singles: sum floor(limit / d) over d in square_divisors
compute pairwise overlaps: for each pair (d_i, d_j), add floor(limit / lcm(d_i, d_j))
apply inclusion-exclusion: total = sum singles - sum pairwise overlaps + sum triple intersections - ...

Floor-Division Multiples.name: Floor-Division Multiples
Floor-Division Multiples.description: Use integer division to count how many multiples of a given divisor lie in 1..N

Shoelace Formula.name: Shoelace Formula
Shoelace Formula.description: compute polygon area from vertex coordinates using the shoelace sum
cues: problem provides explicit coordinates of the polygon's vertices (A, M, C, N)
area can be verified by an alternative method (triangulation)

compute Sum1 = x1*y2 + x2*y3 + x3*y4 + x4*y1
compute Sum2 = y1*x2 + y2*x3 + y3*x4 + y4*x1
area = 1/2 * |Sum1 - Sum2|

Triangulation by diagonal.description: divide polygon AMCN into simpler triangles along a diagonal and sum their areas
cues: region AMCN is a quadrilateral
diagonal AC partitions the region into two triangles ACM and ACN

compute each triangle's area via base-height (see Triangle Area Formula)
sum the two triangle areas to obtain the polygon area

Prime-Subset Product Correspondence.name: Prime-Subset Product Correspondence
Prime-Subset Product Correspondence.description: Each product formed by multiplying distinct members of S (ignoring 1) corresponds bijectively to a nonempty subset of the remaining primes.

Multiplying by 1 does not change the product, so 1 can be ignored
The remaining elements are primes 2, 3, 5, 11

Conversely, every product from S of size ≥ 2 equals the product of a nonempty U ⊆ T

Nonempty subsets of a 4-element set number 2^4 − 1

we seek the count of diagonals (non-side segments between vertices)
problem asks for the count of diagonals in an n-vertex polygon
diagonals count can be obtained directly from the standard formula

diagonals = total_vertex_pairs − n
for n = 7, diagonals = 7×4/2 = 14

Coordinate Setup for Right Trapezoid.name: Coordinate Setup for Right Trapezoid
Coordinate Setup for Right Trapezoid.description: Place the figure on a coordinate plane to exploit parallel bases and perpendicular legs, turning geometric relations into simple distances.

cmath_1005.pseudocode:
We need integer n such that |n| < |n-3| < 9.

1) Solve |n-3| < 9:
   -9 < n - 3 < 9  =>  -6 < n < 12
   So n ∈ { -5, -4, -3, -2, -1, 0, 1, 2, ..., 11 }.

2) Solve |n| < |n-3|:
   Since |n| and |n-3| are nonnegative, we can square:
   n^2 < (n-3)^2 = n^2 - 6n + 9
   0 < -6n + 9  =>  6n < 9  =>  n < 3/2
   So n ≤ 1 for integers.

3) Take the intersection of the two conditions:
   n ∈ { -5, -4, -3, -2, -1, 0, 1 }.

The sum of these integers is:
(-5) + (-4) + (-3) + (-2) + (-1) + 0 + 1 = -14.

Thus, the sum of all integer solutions is \boxed{-14}.

cmath_10055.pseudocode:
Let P(x) = x^{98} + x^{97} + ... + x + 1. Its roots r_1, ..., r_{98} are the 99th roots of unity other than x = 1; i.e., r_i^{99} = 1 and r_i ≠ 1.

We want S = sum_{i=1}^{98} r_i^2/(r_i + 1).

First, observe the identity
r^2/(r+1) = (r-1) + 1/(r+1),
since (r-1) + 1/(r+1) = [(r-1)(r+1) + 1]/(r+1) = r^2/(r+1).

Hence
S = sum_i (r_i - 1) + sum_i 1/(r_i + 1) = (sum_i r_i) - 98 + sum_i 1/(r_i + 1).

By Viète’s formulas, the sum of the roots of P is -1, so sum_i r_i = -1. Thus
S = -1 - 98 + sum_i 1/(r_i + 1) = -99 + sum_i 1/(r_i + 1).

To compute sum_i 1/(r_i + 1), use the standard identity for a polynomial with roots r_i:
P'(a)/P(a) = sum_i 1/(a - r_i).
Taking a = -1 gives
P'(-1)/P(-1) = sum_i 1/(-1 - r_i) = - sum_i 1/(r_i + 1),
so
sum_i 1/(r_i + 1) = - P'(-1)/P(-1).

Compute P(-1) and P'(-1) for P(x) = sum_{k=0}^{98} x^k.

- P(-1) = sum_{k=0}^{98} (-1)^k = 1.
- P'(x) = sum_{k=1}^{98} k x^{k-1}, so P'(-1) = sum_{k=1}^{98} k(-1)^{k-1}.

Pairing terms (1 - 2) + (3 - 4) + ... + (97 - 98) yields 49 pairs each contributing -1, so P'(-1) = -49.

Therefore
sum_i 1/(r_i + 1) = - P'(-1)/P(-1) = -(-49)/1 = 49.

Finally,
S = -99 + 49 = -50.

So the requested sum is \boxed{-50}.

cmath_10114.pseudocode:
Let P(x) = (a+x)(b+x)(c+x). Then P is a monic cubic:
P(x) = x^3 + (a+b+c)x^2 + (ab+bc+ca)x + abc.

Given P(1)=1, P(2)=2, P(3)=3, consider
R(x) = P(x) - x.
Then R(1)=R(2)=R(3)=0, so x-1, x-2, x-3 are roots of R. Since deg R ≤ 3 and its leading coefficient is 1, we must have
R(x) = (x-1)(x-2)(x-3).

Thus
P(x) = x + (x-1)(x-2)(x-3).

Therefore
P(4) = 4 + (4-1)(4-2)(4-3) = 4 + 3·2·1 = 10.

Hence (a+4)(b+4)(c+4) = 10. 

\boxed{10}

cmath_10121.pseudocode:
Let x1, x2, ..., x101 be positive with sum of squares equal to 1:
x1^2 + x2^2 + ... + x101^2 = 1.

Set Q = x2^2 + ... + x101^2 = 1 - x1^2 and S = x2 + x3 + ... + x101. The objective is
f = x1 S.

1) Apply Cauchy-Schwarz to the 100 numbers x2, ..., x101:
S^2 ≤ 100 (x2^2 + ... + x101^2) = 100 Q.
Thus S ≤ 10 sqrt(Q), with equality when x2 = x3 = ... = x101.

2) Therefore for fixed x1,
f ≤ x1 · 10 sqrt(Q) = 10 x1 sqrt(1 - x1^2).
To maximize f, maximize g(x1) = 10 x1 sqrt(1 - x1^2) for x1 ∈ [0,1].

Let y = x1^2. Then
f ≤ 10 sqrt(y(1 - y)),
which attains its maximum when y = 1/2. Hence the maximal value is
f_max = 10 sqrt(1/2 · 1/2) = 10 · 1/2 = 5.

3) Feasibility: equality is achievable when x1^2 = 1/2 and x2 = x3 = ... = x101. Since Q = 1 - x1^2 = 1/2, we need 100 t^2 = 1/2, so t = 1/(10√2). Then S = 100 t = 5√2, and f = x1 S = (1/√2)(5√2) = 5.

Therefore, the maximum value is \boxed{5}.

cmath_10132.pseudocode:
Let z = x + iy, with
z1 = 18 + 83i, z2 = 18 + 39i, z3 = 78 + 99i.

Define A = (z3 − z1)/(z2 − z1). Compute:
z3 − z1 = 60 + 16i, z2 − z1 = −44i, hence
A = (60 + 16i)/(−44i) = (−4 + 15i)/11 = a + bi with a = −4/11, b = 15/11.

Let z − z2 = (x − 18) + (y − 39)i and z − z3 = (x − 78) + (y − 99)i.
Write
B = (z − z2)/(z − z3) = (u + iv)/(s + it),
where u = x − 18, v = y − 39, s = x − 78, t = y − 99.

If AB is real, then Im(AB) = 0. Since A = a + bi, with a = −4/11, b = 15/11, we have
Im(AB) = b Re(B) + a Im(B) = 0.

Compute
Re(B) = (u s + v t)/D, Im(B) = (v s − u t)/D, with D = s^2 + t^2.

Thus
b(u s + v t) + a(v s − u t) = 0.
With a = −4/11, b = 15/11 and multiplying by 11:
15(u s + v t) − 4(v s − u t) = 0.

Substitute u, v, s, t:
u s + v t = (x − 18)(x − 78) + (y − 39)(y − 99) = x^2 + y^2 − 96x − 138y + 5265,
v s − u t = (y − 39)(x − 78) − (x − 18)(y − 99) = 60x − 60y + 1260.

Hence
15[x^2 + y^2 − 96x − 138y + 5265] − 4[60x − 60y + 1260] = 0.

Simplify:
15x^2 + 15y^2 − 1680x − 1830y + 73935 = 0,
which gives
x^2 + y^2 − 112x − 122y + 4929 = 0.

Complete the square:
(x − 56)^2 + (y − 61)^2 = 1928.

Thus the locus of z such that the given expression is real is the circle with center (56, 61) and radius sqrt(1928).

To maximize Im(z), take the topmost point on this circle:
x = 56, y = 61 + sqrt(1928).

Therefore the real part of z is Re(z) = 56, and the answer is
\boxed{56}.

cmath_10133.pseudocode:
Let P(x) = x^4 + (a^2 - 1)x^2 + a^3. Since P is a polynomial in x^2, set y = x^2. Then
P(x) = y^2 + (a^2 - 1)y + a^3.

The roots in x come from y = y1, y2 (the roots of the quadratic in y), giving x^2 = y1 or x^2 = y2. For P(x) to have exactly two distinct complex roots, the set of x-roots must be {r, -r} for some r ≠ 0 (each possibly with multiplicity). This happens precisely when:
- the quadratic in y has a double root y* (so y1 = y2 = y*), and
- y* ≠ 0 (to avoid x = 0 being the only root).

Thus we need the discriminant of y-quadratic to be zero:
Δ_y = (a^2 - 1)^2 - 4a^3 = 0.

Compute:
Δ_y = a^4 - 4a^3 - 2a^2 + 1 = 0.

Factor this quartic as
a^4 - 4a^3 - 2a^2 + 1 = (a^2 + p a + 1)(a^2 + q a + 1),
where p + q = -4 and pq = -4. Solving gives p, q = -2 ± 2√2. Hence the four a-values are the roots of the two quadratics a^2 + ( -2 + 2√2 ) a + 1 = 0 and a^2 + ( -2 - 2√2 ) a + 1 = 0.

Since a = ±1 do not satisfy Δ_y = 0, we have y* ≠ 0 for all these a, so each yields P(x) = (x^2 - y*)^2 and exactly two distinct roots x = ±√y*.

By Vieta’s formula, for the monic polynomial a^4 - 4a^3 - 2a^2 + 1 = 0, the sum of its four roots a is 4.

Therefore, the sum of all complex a for which P(x) has exactly two distinct complex roots is:
\boxed{4}

cmath_10175.pseudocode:
Let P(x) = x^7 − 7, and let its roots be r_1, ..., r_7.

1) Use the resultant trick. For any u, consider Res_x(P(x), P(u − x)). Since P(u − r_i) = ∏_{j=1}^7 (u − r_i − r_j), we have
   Res_x(P(x), P(u − x)) = ∏_{i=1}^7 P(u − r_i) = ∏_{i=1}^7 ∏_{j=1}^7 (u − (r_i + r_j)) = ∏_{i,j} (u − (r_i + r_j)).

   In particular, at u = 0,
   Res_x(P(x), P(−x)) = ∏_{i,j} (−(r_i + r_j)) = (−1)^{49} ∏_{i,j} (r_i + r_j) = − ∏_{i,j} (r_i + r_j).

   Res_x(P(x), P(−x)) = ∏_{i=1}^7 P(−r_i) = (−14)^7.

   Equating the two expressions for the same resultant,
   − ∏_{i,j} (r_i + r_j) = (−14)^7 ⇒ ∏_{i,j} (r_i + r_j) = 14^7.

3) Relate ∏_{i,j} (r_i + r_j) to K. The product over all ordered pairs (i, j) (i, j = 1,…,7) includes:

   Hence

   14^7 = K^2 · 2^7 · 7 ⇒ K^2 = 14^7 / (2^7 · 7) = (2^7 · 7^7) / (2^7 · 7) = 7^6.

cmath_10240.pseudocode:
Let P(x,y) denote the assertion
f(x^2) + f(y^2) = f(x+y)^2 - 2xy for all real x,y.

1) Determine f(0) from P(0,0):
2f(0) = f(0)^2, so f(0) ∈ {0, 2}.

Case 1: f(0) = 0.
- P(x,0) gives f(x^2) = f(x)^2.
- P(x,-x) gives 2f(x^2) = f(0)^2 + 2x^2 = 2x^2, hence f(x^2) = x^2.
- Therefore f(x)^2 = f(x^2) = x^2 for all x, so f(x) ∈ {x, -x} for all x. In particular, for t ≥ 0 (t is a square), t = s^2, so f(t) = f(s^2) = s^2 = t. Thus
  - f(t) = t for all t ≥ 0, and
  - for t < 0, f(t) ∈ {t, -t} (arbitrary choice per t).

It is easy to check these functions satisfy the equation, since
f(x^2) + f(y^2) = x^2 + y^2 and f(x+y)^2 = (x+y)^2, so RHS = (x+y)^2 - 2xy = x^2 + y^2.

Case 2: f(0) = 2.
- P(x,-x) gives 2f(x^2) = f(0)^2 + 2x^2 = 4 + 2x^2, hence f(x^2) = x^2 + 2.
- P(x,0) gives f(x^2) + f(0) = f(x)^2, so f(x)^2 = (x^2 + 2) + 2 = x^2 + 4.
- But for t ≥ 0, t = x^2, we have f(t) = f(x^2) = t + 2. Then f(t)^2 = (t+2)^2, which must equal t^2 + 4 for all t ≥ 0 by the previous line. This is false for any t > 0. Thus Case 2 is impossible.

Therefore the only functions f that can occur satisfy f(0) = 0, f(t) = t for t ≥ 0, and for t < 0, f(t) ∈ {t, -t} (independently for each t).

2) Compute S = sum_{n=-2019}^{2019} f(n).
Let N = 2019. Then
- For n ≥ 0, f(n) = n, so sum_{n=0}^{N} f(n) = sum_{n=0}^{N} n = A, where A = N(N+1)/2 = 2019·2020/2 = 2,039,190.
- For n < 0, write n = -m with m = 1,...,N. Then f(-m) ∈ { -m, m }. Let t_m ∈ { -m, m }. The total negative-contribution is ∑_{m=1}^{N} t_m, which can take any value between -A and A in steps of 2 (since flipping a sign changes the sum by 2m, preserving parity; A = ∑ m).

Hence
S = A + ∑_{m=1}^{N} t_m,
where ∑ t_m ranges over { -A, -A+2, ..., A }. Since A = 2,039,190, S ranges over { 0, 2, 4, ..., 4,078,380 }, i.e., all even integers from 0 to 2A.

The number of possible values of S is
(A + 1) = 2,039,190 + 1 = 2,039,191.

Therefore, the number of possible values of S is \boxed{2039191}.

We want G/(x+5) + H/(x^2 - 4x) = (x^2 - 2x + 10)/(x^3 + x^2 - 20x) for all x ≠ -5, 0, 4.

- Factor denominators:
  - x^2 - 4x = x(x-4)
  - x^3 + x^2 - 20x = x(x+5)(x-4)

- Put the LHS over a common denominator x(x-4)(x+5):
  G/(x+5) = G x(x-4) / [x(x-4)(x+5)]
  H/(x^2 - 4x) = H (x+5) / [x(x-4)(x+5)]
  Thus LHS = [G x(x-4) + H (x+5)] / [x(x-4)(x+5)]

- The RHS already has the same denominator, so we equate numerators:
  G x(x-4) + H(x+5) = x^2 - 2x + 10

- Expand:
  G(x^2 - 4x) + Hx + 5H = G x^2 + (-4G + H)x + 5H

- Match coefficients with x^2 - 2x + 10:
  - x^2: G = 1
  - x: -4G + H = -2
  - constant: 5H = 10

- From 5H = 10, H = 2. With G = 1, the x-coefficient equation gives -4(1) + 2 = -2, which is consistent.

Therefore G = 1 and H = 2, so H/G = 2.

\boxed{2}

Let f(x,y,z) = 3x^2 + 12y^2 + 27z^2 - 4xy - 6xz - 12yz - 8y - 24z.

1) Recognize this as a quadratic form. The Hessian (matrix of second partials) is
A = [[3, -2, -3],
     [-2, 12, -6],
     [-3, -6, 27]].
The linear term is b = [0, -8, -24].

- By Sylvester’s criterion, the leading principal minors are
D1 = 3 > 0,
D2 = det[[3,-2],[-2,12]] = 3·12 - (-2)(-2) = 32 > 0,
Det A = 576 > 0.
Thus A is positive definite, so f is strictly convex and has a unique global minimum at the critical point where ∇f = 0.

2) Compute the gradient and solve ∇f = 0:
∂f/∂x = 6x - 4y - 6z = 0  ->  3x - 2y - 3z = 0  ->  x = (2/3)y + z
∂f/∂y = 24y - 4x - 12z - 8 = 0 -> -4x + 24y - 12z = 8
∂f/∂z = 54z - 6x - 12y - 24 = 0 -> -6x - 12y + 54z = 24

Substitute x = (2/3)y + z into the last two equations and simplify:

- From ∂f/∂y = 0, after substitution:
16y - 12z = 6  ->  4y - 3z = 1.5
- From ∂f/∂z = 0, after substitution:
-8y + 24z = 12  ->  -2y + 6z = 3

Solving:
From -2y + 6z = 3  ->  y = 3z - 1.5
Plug into 4y - 3z = 1.5:
4(3z - 1.5) - 3z = 1.5
12z - 6 - 3z = 1.5
9z = 7.5  ->  z = 5/6
Then y = 3(5/6) - 3/2 = 5/2 - 3/2 = 1
Finally x = (2/3)y + z = (2/3)·1 + 5/6 = 2/3 + 5/6 = 9/6 = 3/2

So the minimizer is (x, y, z) = (3/2, 1, 5/6).

3) Compute the minimum value:
f(3/2, 1, 5/6) = 3(9/4) + 12(1) + 27(25/36) - 4(3/2)(1) - 6(3/2)(5/6) - 12(1)(5/6) - 8(1) - 24(5/6)
= 27/4 + 12 + 75/4 - 6 - 7.5 - 10 - 8 - 20
= -14.

Therefore, the minimum value is -14.

Answer: \boxed{-14}

c2 = ∑_{1 ≤ i < j ≤ 15} a_i a_j.

A convenient identity is
∑_{i<j} a_i a_j = ( (∑ a_i)^2 − ∑ a_i^2 ) / 2.

cmath_10392.pseudocode:
Let α = √2 + √3 + √5. We will find its minimal polynomial P(x) over Q and then compute P(1).

1) First combine two radicals.
Let y = √2 + √3. Then
y^2 = (√2 + √3)^2 = 2 + 3 + 2√6 = 5 + 2√6.
Hence (y^2 − 5)^2 = (2√6)^2 = 24, so
y^4 − 10y^2 + 1 = 0.      (1)

2) Express α in terms of y and t = √5.
We have α = y + t with t^2 = 5.

3) Substitute y = α − t into (1) and eliminate t.
Compute f(t) = (α − t)^4 − 10(α − t)^2 + 1.
Expand and then reduce using t^2 = 5, t^3 = 5t, t^4 = 25:
f(t) = (α^4 + 20α^2 − 24) + (−4α^3)t.
Since f(t) = 0 and t = √5, we obtain
4α^3 t = α^4 + 20α^2 − 24.
Square both sides and use t^2 = 5:
16α^6 t^2 = (α^4 + 20α^2 − 24)^2
⇒ 80α^6 = (α^4 + 20α^2 − 24)^2.

4) Obtain the polynomial in α.
Let x = α and u = x^2. Then (x^4 + 20x^2 − 24)^2 − 80x^6 = 0 becomes
u^4 − 40u^3 + 352u^2 − 960u + 576 = 0
with u = x^2. Thus the polynomial in x is
P(x) = x^8 − 40x^6 + 352x^4 − 960x^2 + 576.

This is monic of degree 8 with rational coefficients, and α is a root; hence P is the required polynomial.

5) Compute P(1).
P(1) = 1 − 40 + 352 − 960 + 576 = -71.

Therefore, the answer is
\boxed{-71}.

Let P(x,y,z) denote the assertion
f(x + f(y + z)) + f(f(x + y) + z) = 2y, with f(1) = 1.

- C/B = r and D/C = r, so C/B = D/C = r.
Given C/B = 5/3, we have r = 5/3.

From D = Cr, we get D = C*(5/3). Since D must be an integer, C must be divisible by 3.

Also A, B, C are in arithmetic progression, so
2B = A + C, hence A = 2B − C.

Let B = 3x to make C = (5/3)B an integer. Then C = 5x, and
D = Cr = (5x)*(5/3) = (25/3)x.

- B = 3x = 9m
- C = 5x = 15m
- D = 25m

Now A = 2B − C = 18m − 15m = 3m.

All four are positive integers: (A,B,C,D) = (3m, 9m, 15m, 25m). The sum is

cmath_10456.pseudocode:
Let d = a − b > 0 and s = a + b. Then
- (a + b)² − (a − b)² = 4ab ⇒ s² = d² + 4ab = d² + 32.
- a² + b² = (a + b)² − 2ab = s² − 16 = (d² + 32) − 16 = d² + 16.

Thus the expression becomes
E = (a² + b²)/(a − b) = (d² + 16)/d = d + 16/d, for d > 0.

Minimize f(d) = d + 16/d on d > 0. By AM-GM (or calculus), the minimum occurs at d = √16 = 4, giving
f(4) = 4 + 16/4 = 8.

The minimum is attained, for example, when d = a − b = 4 and ab = 8 (one can take a = 2√3 + 2, b = 2√3 − 2).

Therefore, the minimum value is \boxed{8}.

cmath_1047.pseudocode:
Let the common speed be S mph.

- Jack’s speed: S = x^2 - 11x - 22
- Jill’s speed: S = (distance)/(time) = (x^2 - 3x - 54)/(x + 6)

Set them equal:
(x^2 - 11x - 22)(x + 6) = x^2 - 3x - 54

Expand left:
x^3 - 5x^2 - 88x - 132 = x^2 - 3x - 54

Bring all terms to one side:
x^3 - 6x^2 - 85x - 78 = 0

Factor the cubic. By the Rational Root Theorem, test x = -1:
(-1)^3 - 6(-1)^2 - 85(-1) - 78 = -1 - 6 + 85 - 78 = 0,
so (x + 1) is a factor. Divide:
x^3 - 6x^2 - 85x - 78 = (x + 1)(x^2 - 7x - 78)

Factor the quadratic:
x^2 - 7x - 78 = (x - 13)(x + 6)

Thus the roots are x = -1, x = 13, x = -6.

Domain check: x ≠ -6 (denominator x+6). Also, x = -1 gives negative speed:
S = (-1)^2 - 11(-1) - 22 = 1 + 11 - 22 = -10 mph, which is not physical.

So x = 13 is valid. Compute the speed:
S = x^2 - 11x - 22 = 13^2 - 11·13 - 22 = 169 - 143 - 22 = 4 mph.

Answer: \boxed{4}

Reasoning:

- A unit fraction 1/k terminates in decimal iff k has no prime factors other than 2 and 5. Equivalently, k is of the form k = 2^a 5^b for some nonnegative integers a,b.

- Let H(n) be the number of integers k with 1 ≤ k ≤ n that are of the form 2^a 5^b (i.e., whose decimal terminates).

- We need H(n) = n/2 with n as small as possible.

- Check small n (even ones are the only candidates since n/2 must be integer):
  - For n = 2: the terminating k are {1,2} → H(2) = 2, and n/2 = 1. Not equal.
  - n = 4: terminating k are {1,2,4} → H(4) = 3, n/2 = 2. Not equal.
  - n = 6: terminating k are {1,2,4,5} → H(6) = 4, n/2 = 3. Not equal.

  - n = 12: terminating k are {1,2,4,5,8,10} within 1..12 → H(12) = 6, and n/2 = 6. Equal.

cmath_10561.pseudocode:
Let x = a − 5 and y = a + 1. Then y − x = 6 and
- gcd(x, y) = gcd(a − 5, a + 1) = gcd(a − 5, 6) ∈ {1, 2, 3, 6},
- lcm(x, y) = 10508.

Using the identity lcm(x, y) · gcd(x, y) = x · y, we have
x y = 10508 · gcd(x, y) = 10508 · d, where d ∈ {1, 2, 3, 6} and gcd(x, y) = d.

Note that 10508 = 2^2 · 37 · 71, so 10508 is even but not divisible by 3.

1) Exclude d = 1: If gcd(x, y) = 1, then x and y are coprime and differ by 6. Since they have the same parity, either both are even or both are odd. They cannot both be even (then gcd would be at least 2), and if both are odd, their product would be odd, contradicting x y = 10508.

2) Exclude d = 3 or 6: If d is 3 or 6, then both x and y are multiples of 3, so lcm(x, y) would be a multiple of 3, contradicting 10508 ∉ multiples of 3.

Thus the only possibility is d = 2.

Let x = 2u, y = 2u + 6. Then
lcm(x, y) = (x y)/2 = (2u)(2u + 6)/2 = 2u(u + 3) = 10508,
so u(u + 3) = 10508 / 2 = 5254 = 2 · 37 · 71.

We need two integers differing by 3 whose product is 5254. The factor pairs of 5254 are:
- (1, 5254) → diff 5253
- (2, 2627) → diff 2625
- (37, 142) → diff 105
- (71, 74) → diff 3

Thus u = 71 works, giving x = 2u = 142 and y = x + 6 = 148. Therefore
a − 5 = 142 ⇒ a = 147.

Finally compute a^2 − 4a + 1:
147^2 − 4·147 + 1 = 21609 − 588 + 1 = 21022.

Let n be a positive odd integer less than 2010, and consider the fraction 1/n in lowest terms (gcd(1,n)=1). A fraction a/b in lowest terms has a terminating decimal expansion if and only if b has no prime factors other than 2 and 5.

Since our denominator is n and n is odd, n cannot contain the factor 2. Therefore, for 1/n to terminate, n must be of the form 5^k for some k ≥ 0.

Find all odd n < 2010 of this form:
- 5^0 = 1
- 5^1 = 5
- 5^2 = 25
- 5^3 = 125
- 5^4 = 625
- 5^5 = 3125 (too large)

Thus there are 5 favorable odd integers: {1, 5, 25, 125, 625}.

Total number of positive odd integers less than 2010 is the count of odd numbers from 1 to 2009, which is 1005.

Probability = favorable / total = 5 / 1005. Reduce this fraction:
5/1005 = 1/201.

Thus a = 1, b = 201, and a + b = 1 + 201 = 202.

\boxed{202}

We seek the number of fractions n/99 with 0 < n < 99 that are in lowest terms. This is equivalent to counting n with gcd(n, 99) = 1 for n = 1, 2, ..., 98.

- Multiples of 3: floor(98/3) = 32
- Multiples of 11: floor(98/11) = 8
- Multiples of both (i.e., multiples of lcm(3,11) = 33): floor(98/33) = 2

So the numbers not divisible by 3 or 11 is:

cmath_10619.pseudocode:
We need numbers with exactly four positive divisors. If n factors as n = p1^a1 p2^a2 …, then the number of divisors is tau(n) = (a1+1)(a2+1)… For tau(n) = 4, the exponents must multiply to 4. The possibilities are:

- One prime to the third power: n = p^3 (since 3+1 = 4)
- Product of two distinct primes: n = pq with p ≠ q (since (1+1)(1+1) = 4)

Thus all such numbers are either p^3 or pq with p, q primes.

Now list the smallest such numbers:

- Smallest p^3: 2^3 = 8
- Smallest pq: 2·3 = 6, then 2·5 = 10, then 2·7 = 14, then 3·5 = 15, ...

Sort the first few: 6, 8, 10, 14, 15, ...

These are indeed the five smallest numbers with exactly four divisors. Their sum is:
6 + 8 + 10 + 14 + 15 = 53.

\boxed{53}

cmath_10631.pseudocode:
A five-digit palindrome has the form abcba, where a is nonzero.

A number is divisible by 11 if and only if the alternating sum of its digits is a multiple of 11:
d1 − d2 + d3 − d4 + d5 ≡ 0 (mod 11).

For abcba, this becomes:
a − b + c − b + a = 2a + c − 2b ≡ 0 (mod 11).

To minimize, take the smallest possible a, namely a = 1. Then
2a + c − 2b = 2 + c − 2b ≡ 0 (mod 11) ⇒ c ≡ −(2) + 2b ≡ 2b − 2 (mod 11).

We want c to be a digit (0 ≤ c ≤ 9). To get the smallest palindrome, choose the smallest b feasible. Try b = 0:
c ≡ 2(0) − 2 ≡ −2 ≡ 9 (mod 11), so c = 9 (since 0 ≤ c ≤ 9).

Thus the smallest palindrome is 1 0 9 0 1 = 10901. It is divisible by 11 since 10901 / 11 = 991.

Therefore, the smallest five-digit palindrome divisible by 11 is \boxed{10901}.

where d ∈ {0,1,2,3,4,5,6,7}.

Sum all possible n:
Sum_{d=0}^{7} (545 + 64d) = 8·545 + 64·(0+1+...+7) = 4360 + 64·28 = 4360 + 1792 = 6152.

Answer: \boxed{6152}

cmath_10667.pseudocode:
Let P(n) = n(n+1)(n+2)(n+3) be the product of four consecutive positive integers.

1) Divisibility by 24 for every n.
- Among four consecutive integers, there are exactly two even numbers. They are consecutive even numbers e and e+2; one of them is divisible by 4. Hence the product P(n) is divisible by 2 × 4 = 8.
- Among any four consecutive integers, there is at least one multiple of 3, so P(n) is divisible by 3.

Therefore P(n) is divisible by 8 × 3 = 24 for every n.

2) The gcd cannot exceed 24.
- Note P(1) = 1·2·3·4 = 24. The gcd of the entire set must divide every element, in particular it divides 24. Since every element is divisible by 24, the gcd is at least 24 and cannot be larger than 24.

Thus the greatest common divisor of all such products is 24.

Answer: \boxed{24}

cmath_10674.pseudocode:
Let a, b, c be nonzero residues modulo 13 (since they are in {1,2,...,12}).

Introduce
- p = ab
- q = bc
- r = ca
- S = abc

The given congruences become linear in p, q, r, S:
1) 2p + q + r ≡ 0 (mod 13)
2) p + 2q + r ≡ 6S (mod 13)
3) p + q + 2r ≡ 8S (mod 13)

Step 1: Eliminate p, q, r in terms of S
From (2) − (1): (p + 2q + r) − (2p + q + r) ≡ −p + q ≡ 6S, so
q ≡ p + 6S.  (A)

From (3) − (1): (p + q + 2r) − (2p + q + r) ≡ −p + r ≡ 8S, so
r ≡ p + 8S.  (B)

Substitute (A) and (B) into (1):
2p + (p + 6S) + (p + 8S) ≡ 0
4p + 14S ≡ 0
Since 14 ≡ 1 (mod 13), 4p + S ≡ 0, hence
p ≡ −S·4^{-1} ≡ −S·10 ≡ 3S (mod 13)  (since 4^{-1} ≡ 10)

Then from (A) and (B):
q ≡ p + 6S ≡ 3S + 6S ≡ 9S
r ≡ p + 8S ≡ 3S + 8S ≡ 11S

Thus for any solution we must have
ab ≡ p ≡ 3S,  bc ≡ q ≡ 9S,  ca ≡ r ≡ 11S,  with S ≡ abc (mod 13).

Step 2: Use pqr = (ab)(bc)(ca) = a^2 b^2 c^2 = S^2
Compute pqr modulo 13 using p,q,r in terms of S:
pqr ≡ (3S)(9S)(11S) = (3·9·11) S^3 = 297 S^3 ≡ 11 S^3 (mod 13)

Hence S^2 ≡ 11 S^3 (mod 13). Since S ≠ 0 (a,b,c are nonzero mod 13), we can divide by S^2:
1 ≡ 11 S (mod 13) ⇒ S ≡ 11^{-1} ≡ 6 (mod 13)

Therefore abc ≡ S ≡ 6 (mod 13).

Step 3: Determine ab, bc, ca with S ≡ 6
From p ≡ 3S, q ≡ 9S, r ≡ 11S:
ab ≡ 3·6 ≡ 5 (mod 13)
bc ≡ 9·6 ≡ 54 ≡ 2 (mod 13)
ca ≡ 11·6 ≡ 66 ≡ 1 (mod 13)

Step 4: Solve for (a,b,c) from
ab ≡ 5,  bc ≡ 2,  ca ≡ 1 (mod 13)

From bc/ab = c/a ≡ 2/5 ≡ 3 (mod 13), so c ≡ 3a.
From ca ≡ 1, we have (3a)a ≡ 1 ⇒ 3a^2 ≡ 1 (mod 13) ⇒ a^2 ≡ 9 (mod 13) ⇒ a ≡ 3 or a ≡ −3 ≡ 10 (mod 13).

- If a ≡ 3, then b ≡ 5 a^{-1} ≡ 5·9 ≡ 6, and c ≡ 3a ≡ 9.
  So (a,b,c) ≡ (3,6,9) (mod 13). Then abc ≡ 3·6·9 ≡ 162 ≡ 6, which is consistent with S ≡ 6.

- If a ≡ 10, then b ≡ 5 a^{-1} ≡ 5·4 ≡ 7, and c ≡ 3a ≡ 4.
  Then abc ≡ 10·7·4 ≡ 280 ≡ 7, which contradicts S ≡ 6, so this case is invalid.

Thus the unique solution modulo 13 is a ≡ 3, b ≡ 6, c ≡ 9.

Step 5: Find a+b+c mod 13
a + b + c ≡ 3 + 6 + 9 ≡ 18 ≡ 5 (mod 13).

Answer: \boxed{5}

cmath_10686.pseudocode:
We want to solve 14u ≡ 46 (mod 100).

- Compute d = gcd(14, 100) = 2. Since d | 46, solutions exist. There are d = 2 incongruent solutions modulo 100.
- Divide by d: (14/2)u ≡ (46/2) (mod 100/2) ⇒ 7u ≡ 23 (mod 50).
- Since gcd(7, 50) = 1, 7 has an inverse modulo 50. The inverse is 43 because 7·43 = 301 ≡ 1 (mod 50).
- Multiply: u ≡ 43·23 ≡ 989 ≡ 39 (mod 50).

Thus the solutions modulo 100 are u ≡ 39 or u ≡ 39+50 ≡ 89 (mod 100). The two smallest positive solutions are 39 and 89.

Their average is (39 + 89)/2 = 128/2 = 64.

cmath_10691.pseudocode:
Let C(n) be the correct answer for item n, and S(n) the student’s answer.

- C(n) = True if n is a multiple of 4; otherwise False.
- S(n) = False if n is a multiple of 3; otherwise True.

We want the count of n in {1,2,...,100} for which C(n) = S(n).

Periodicity: C(n) depends on n mod 4 and S(n) depends on n mod 3, so the combined pattern repeats with period lcm(3,4) = 12. It suffices to analyze n = 1,...,12, then repeat 8 times (since 100 = 12*8 + 4) and handle the remaining 4 terms.

Compute for n = 1 to 12:
- C(n) is True exactly for n ∈ {4,8,12}; False otherwise.
- S(n) is False exactly for n ∈ {3,6,9,12}; True otherwise.

Matches (C(n) = S(n)) occur for n = 3, 4, 6, 8, 9. Thus there are 5 matches in each block of 12.

- Number of full 12-blocks in 1..100: 8. Matches from full blocks: 8 × 5 = 40.
- Remaining items: n = 97, 98, 99, 100 (which correspond to residues 1, 2, 3, 4 mod 12). From the 1..12 analysis, these give matches for n = 99 and 100, i.e., 2 more matches.

Total correct answers = 40 + 2 = 42.

Therefore, the final answer is \boxed{42}.

cmath_10693.pseudocode:
We want to solve 31n ≡ 3 (mod 2293). This requires the modular inverse of 31 modulo 2293.

Use the extended Euclidean algorithm:
- 2293 = 31·73 + 30
- 31 = 30·1 + 1
- 30 = 1·30 + 0

Back-substitute to express 1 as a combination of 2293 and 31:
- 1 = 31 − 30·1
- 30 = 2293 − 31·73
Thus 1 = 31 − (2293 − 31·73) = 31·74 − 2293

Therefore 31·74 ≡ 1 (mod 2293), so the modular inverse of 31 modulo 2293 is 74.

Now solve for n:
n ≡ 3 · 74 ≡ 222 (mod 2293)

Since 0 ≤ n < 2293, the requested n is:
\boxed{222}

cmath_10704.pseudocode:
Let N be the number of Penteria alive at the very beginning (time 0).

- The population grows by 5 per minute, so in any hour after m minutes (0 ≤ m ≤ 60), the number would be N + 5m just before the end of that hour.
- At the end of every hour, all but the initial ones die. That means after each hour ends, the number alive is reset to the number that were alive at the start of that hour, which is N. So immediately after the end of each full hour, the population is N again.

506 minutes is 8 full hours (8 × 60 = 480) plus 26 minutes into the 9th hour. Since the killing events occur only at hour boundaries, at t = 506 minutes the population is still growing within the 9th hour and equals:
N + 5 × 26 = N + 130.

We’re told that 137 are alive after 506 minutes, so:
N + 130 = 137
N = 7.

Thus the initial population was \boxed{7}.

But among any two consecutive integers, one is even. Since 20 has the factor 2, at least one of a or a-1 is even, so at least one of gcd(a,20), gcd(a-1,20) is divisible by 2 and hence not equal to 1.   a^2 ≡ 4(a-1) (mod 20)

cmath_10821.pseudocode:
We want to solve 27a ≡ 17 (mod 40).

- Since gcd(27, 40) = 1, 27 has a modular inverse modulo 40. Use the Extended Euclidean Algorithm:
  - 40 = 27·1 + 13
  - 27 = 13·2 + 1
  - 13 = 40 − 27
  Back-substitute: 1 = 27 − 2·13 = 27 − 2(40 − 27) = 3·27 − 2·40.
  Thus 3·27 ≡ 1 (mod 40), so the inverse of 27 modulo 40 is 3.

- Multiply both sides of 27a ≡ 17 (mod 40) by 3:
  a ≡ 3·17 ≡ 51 ≡ 11 (mod 40).

Therefore, the solutions are a ≡ 11 (mod 40). The smallest positive solution is a = 11, and the second smallest is a = 11 + 40 = 51.

Sum = 11 + 51 = 62.

\boxed{62}

cmath_10828.pseudocode:
Let a be an integer with -200 ≤ a ≤ -1. Write a = -n where n ∈ {1,2,...,200}. The divisors of a are exactly {±d : d | n} (for every positive divisor d of n).

- Pair each divisor d with its negative -d. The product over a pair is (-d)(d) = -d^2.
- Hence the product P(a) of all divisors of a equals
  P(a) = ∏_{d|n} (-d^2) = (-1)^{τ(n)} ∏_{d|n} d^2,
  where τ(n) is the number of positive divisors of n.
- Using the standard result that the product of all positive divisors of n is ∏_{d|n} d = n^{τ(n)/2}, we get
  P(a) = (-1)^{τ(n)} (n^{τ(n)/2})^2 = (-1)^{τ(n)} n^{τ(n)}.

Thus the sign of the product of the divisors of a depends on τ(n): P(a) is negative iff τ(n) is odd, which happens exactly when n is a perfect square.

Therefore we need n to be a perfect square with 1 ≤ n ≤ 200. The squares are 1^2, 2^2, ..., 14^2 (since 15^2 = 225 > 200). That gives 14 values of n, hence 14 corresponding a = -n.

Answer: \boxed{14}.

cmath_10854.pseudocode:
We want the largest integer that necessarily divides mn given:
- m ≡ 6 (mod 9)
- n ≡ 0 (mod 9)

1) From m ≡ 6 (mod 9): m = 9k + 6 = 3(3k + 2). The factor 3(3k+2) shows m is divisible by 3, and 3k+2 ≡ 2 (mod 3), so m is not divisible by 9. Hence the exact power of 3 in m is v3(m) = 1.

2) From n ≡ 0 (mod 9): n = 9r, so v3(n) ≥ 2.

3) For mn, the power of 3 satisfies v3(mn) = v3(m) + v3(n) ≥ 1 + 2 = 3. Therefore 3^3 = 27 divides mn for all such m and n. So mn is always a multiple of 27.

4) To check maximality: if you try to guarantee a larger divisor, say 81 = 3^4, you can choose m = 6 (v3(m) = 1) and n = 9 (v3(n) = 2), giving mn = 54, which is not divisible by 81. Hence 81 does not necessarily divide mn, so 27 is the largest possible.

Answer: \boxed{27}

cmath_10860.pseudocode:
Compute the prime factorization of N = 3! · 5! · 7!.

- 3! = 6 = 2^1 · 3^1
- 5! = 120 = 2^3 · 3^1 · 5^1
- 7! = 5040 = 2^4 · 3^2 · 5^1 · 7^1

Multiply them (add exponents for each prime):
N = 2^(1+3+4) · 3^(1+1+2) · 5^(0+1+1) · 7^1 = 2^8 · 3^4 · 5^2 · 7^1.

A divisor d of N is a cube if and only if its prime exponents are multiples of 3. If N = ∏ p^e, the number of cube divisors is ∏ ( floor(e/3) + 1 ).

Apply to N:
- e2 = 8 → floor(8/3) + 1 = 2 + 1 = 3 choices for the 2-exponent (0,3,6)
- e3 = 4 → floor(4/3) + 1 = 1 + 1 = 2 choices for the 3-exponent (0,3)
- e5 = 2 → floor(2/3) + 1 = 0 + 1 = 1 choice (0)
- e7 = 1 → floor(1/3) + 1 = 0 + 1 = 1 choice (0)

Total number of cube divisors = 3 · 2 · 1 · 1 = 6.

Explicit cube divisors: 1, 8, 64, 27, 216, 1728 (i.e., 2^a 3^b with a ∈ {0,3,6}, b ∈ {0,3}).

\boxed{6}

cmath_10905.pseudocode:
Let ABC be digits with A ∈ {1,2,3} (leading digit in base 4), B ∈ {0,1,2,3}, C ∈ {0,1,2,3} (since digits must be valid in both base 4 and base 9).

Convert to decimal:
- ABC_4 = 16A + 4B + C
- ABC_9 = 81A + 9B + C

Given: ABC_4 + 200 = ABC_9
So 16A + 4B + C + 200 = 81A + 9B + C

Cancel C:
16A + 4B + 200 = 81A + 9B
200 = 65A + 5B
Divide by 5: 40 = 13A + B
Thus B = 40 − 13A.

Check possible A values:
- A = 1 ⇒ B = 27 (not a valid base-4 digit)
- A = 2 ⇒ B = 14 (not valid)
- A = 3 ⇒ B = 1 (valid)

So the only possibility is A = 3, B = 1. C is unrestricted among digits common to both bases, i.e., C ∈ {0,1,2,3}.

Therefore:
- A can be {3} ⇒ sum_A = 3
- B can be {1} ⇒ sum_B = 1
- C can be {0,1,2,3} ⇒ sum_C = 0 + 1 + 2 + 3 = 6

Total sum = sum_A + sum_B + sum_C = 3 + 1 + 6 = 10.

\boxed{10}

We work modulo m = 7.

- First compute L = (a+b)^{-1} with a=2, b=3. Then a+b = 5. We seek x such that 5x ≡ 1 (mod 7). Using the extended Euclidean algorithm:
  7 = 1·5 + 2
  5 = 2·2 + 1
  Back-substitute: 1 = 5 − 2·2 = 5 − 2(7 − 1·5) = 3·5 − 2·7
  Hence 3·5 ≡ 1 (mod 7), so L = 3.

- Now compute R = a^{-1} + b^{-1} mod 7.
  2^{-1} ≡ 4 since 2·4 = 8 ≡ 1 (mod 7).
  3^{-1} ≡ 5 since 3·5 = 15 ≡ 1 (mod 7).

cmath_10946.pseudocode:
We note that a ≡ 8 (mod 9) already implies a ≡ 2 (mod 3) since 8 ≡ 2 (mod 3). So the system reduces to the pairwise coprime moduli 9, 5, and 7:

- a ≡ 8 (mod 9)
- a ≡ 4 (mod 5)
- a ≡ 6 (mod 7)

Use the Chinese Remainder Theorem (CRT) step by step.

1) Solve a ≡ 8 (mod 9) and a ≡ 4 (mod 5).
Let a = 8 + 9t. Then 8 + 9t ≡ 4 (mod 5) → 3 + 4t ≡ 4 → 4t ≡ 1 (mod 5) → t ≡ 4 (mod 5).
So t = 4 + 5k, hence a = 8 + 9(4 + 5k) = 44 + 45k.
Thus a ≡ 44 (mod 45).

2) Combine with a ≡ 6 (mod 7).
Let a = 44 + 45m. Then modulo 7: 44 ≡ 2 and 45 ≡ 3, so 2 + 3m ≡ 6 (mod 7) → 3m ≡ 4 (mod 7).
The inverse of 3 mod 7 is 5, so m ≡ 4·5 ≡ 6 (mod 7).
Thus m = 6 + 7t, and a = 44 + 45(6 + 7t) = 44 + 270 + 315t = 314 + 315t.

Hence a ≡ 314 (mod 315). The smallest nonnegative solution is a = 314.

Check: 314 ≡ 8 (mod 9), 314 ≡ 4 (mod 5), 314 ≡ 6 (mod 7), and hence ≡ 2 (mod 3) as required.

Therefore, the answer is \boxed{314}.

cmath_10965.pseudocode:
Let T be the smallest positive multiple of 14 whose digits are only 0 or 1.

1) Since T must be even, its last digit is 0. Write T = 10·M, where M is a decimal number whose digits are only 0 or 1 (and M starts with 1).

2) Since 14 | T = 10·M and gcd(10,14) = 2, we have
   14 | 10M ⇔ (dividing by 2) 7 | 5M.
   Because gcd(5,7) = 1, this is equivalent to 7 | M.

Thus M must be a positive integer consisting of digits 0 and 1, with first digit 1, that is divisible by 7. We seek the smallest such M (to minimize T).

3) Check numbers with digits 0/1 by increasing length:
- Length 1: 1 → 1 mod 7
- Length 2: 10 → 3; 11 → 4
- Length 3: 100 → 2; 101 → 3; 110 → 5; 111 → 6
- Length 4: 1000 → 6; 1001 → 0

We find M = 1001 is the smallest (length 4) number composed of 0s and 1s that is divisible by 7 (since 1001 = 7 · 143).

4) Therefore T = 10·M = 10010, which is divisible by 14. The quotient is
   T/14 = (10·M)/14 = (5·M)/7 = 5·143 = 715.

Answer: \boxed{715}

b^5 + b^2 has coefficient 1 at b^5 and at b^2, with zeros elsewhere. Therefore the base-b numeral is 100100_b.

Final answer (boxed as requested): \boxed{100100} 

Optional check (valid for any base b):
- Take b = 10: 11011_10 × 9 + 1001_10 = 11011 × 9 + 1001 = 99099 + 1001 = 100100, which matches 100100_b when b = 10.

cmath_11028.pseudocode:
Let P be the product of all primes between 1 and 100. Since 2 is the only even prime in this range, write
P = 2 · R, where R is the product of all odd primes ≤ 100. Then P is even but not divisible by 4, so P ≡ 2 mod 4, and we will determine P mod 16.

Step 1: Reduce R modulo 8.
For each odd prime p ≤ 100, p ≡ 1, 3, 5, or 7 (mod 8). Let:
- a = number of primes with p ≡ 3 (mod 8),
- b = number with p ≡ 5 (mod 8),
- c = number with p ≡ 7 (mod 8),
- d = number with p ≡ 1 (mod 8).

Then
R ≡ 3^a · 5^b · 7^c · 1^d (mod 8).

From listing the odd primes ≤ 100, we have:
a = 7, b = 6, c = 6, d = 5.

Thus
R ≡ 3^7 · 5^6 · 7^6 (mod 8).

Compute each factor modulo 8:
- 3^2 ≡ 1 (mod 8) ⇒ 3^7 ≡ 3 (mod 8),
- 5^2 ≡ 1 (mod 8) ⇒ 5^6 ≡ 1 (mod 8),
- 7^2 ≡ 1 (mod 8) ⇒ 7^6 ≡ 1 (mod 8).

Therefore R ≡ 3 · 1 · 1 ≡ 3 (mod 8).

Step 2: Get P modulo 16.
P ≡ 2 · R ≡ 2 · 3 ≡ 6 (mod 16).

Hence the remainder when P is divided by 16 is 6.

\boxed{6}

cmath_11156.pseudocode:
Let the teams be A, B, C, each with 4 players.

- Each such pair shakes hands once.
- With 3 teams: 3 × 6 = 18 handshakes.

2) Handshakes between different teams:
- Between any two teams (e.g., A and B), there are 4 × 4 = 16 unordered pairs of players.
- There are 3 such inter-team pairings: AB, AC, BC, for a total of 3 × 16 = 48 unordered pairs.
- Each cross-team pair shakes hands 3 times.
- So cross-team handshakes: 48 × 3 = 144.

Total handshakes = 18 (within) + 144 (between) = 162.

Sanity check (per-person count):
- Each person shakes hands with 3 teammates (within their team) and with 8 players from the other teams, 3 times each: 3 + 8×3 = 27 handshakes per person.
- With 12 people total, sum would be 12×27 = 324, but each handshake is counted twice (once per participant), so 324/2 = 162.

Final answer: \boxed{162}

cmath_11166.pseudocode:
We want the exponent of the prime 3 in 109!. Use Legendre’s formula (also known as de Polignac’s formula): for a prime p and n!, the exponent of p in n! is

sum_{k≥1} floor(n / p^k).

Here p = 3 and n = 109. Compute the terms:

- floor(109 / 3) = 36
- floor(109 / 9) = 12
- floor(109 / 27) = 4
- floor(109 / 81) = 1
- floor(109 / 243) = 0 (and higher powers give 0)

Sum: 36 + 12 + 4 + 1 = 53.

Thus the exponent of 3 in 109! is 53.

\boxed{53}

cmath_11357.pseudocode:
Let a 3-digit palindrome be written as aba, where a ∈ {1,...,9} and b ∈ {0,...,9}. The number is 100a + 10b + a = 101a + 10b.

A number is divisible by 3 iff the sum of its digits is divisible by 3. For aba, the digit sum is a + b + a = 2a + b. So we require
2a + b ≡ 0 (mod 3).

Since 2 ≡ −1 (mod 3), this is equivalent to
−a + b ≡ 0 (mod 3) ⇒ b ≡ a (mod 3).

Now count possibilities:
- If a ≡ 0 (mod 3), i.e., a ∈ {3,6,9}, then b must be ≡ 0 (mod 3), giving b ∈ {0,3,6,9} → 4 choices.
- If a ≡ 1 (mod 3), i.e., a ∈ {1,4,7}, then b ≡ 1 (mod 3), giving b ∈ {1,4,7} → 3 choices.
- If a ≡ 2 (mod 3), i.e., a ∈ {2,5,8}, then b ≡ 2 (mod 3), giving b ∈ {2,5,8} → 3 choices.

Among a ∈ {1,...,9}, there are 3 numbers in each residue class mod 3. Therefore, the total number is
(3 choices for a ≡ 0) × (4 b choices) + (3 choices for a ≡ 1) × (3 b choices) + (3 choices for a ≡ 2) × (3 b choices)
= 3·4 + 3·3 + 3·3 = 12 + 9 + 9 = 30.

Thus, there are \boxed{30} positive 3-digit palindromes that are multiples of 3.

cmath_11433.pseudocode:
We want gcd(n, 36) = 18 for the smallest n > 200.

- Factor 36: 36 = 2^2 · 3^2.
- Let n have prime exponents v2(n) and v3(n) for the primes 2 and 3 (other primes don’t affect gcd with 36).
- Since gcd(n,36) = 18 = 2^1 · 3^2, we must have:
  - min(v2(n), 2) = 1, so v2(n) = 1 (n is even but not divisible by 4).
  - min(v3(n), 2) = 2, so v3(n) ≥ 2 (n is divisible by 9).

Thus n must be divisible by 18 but not by 36. Equivalently, n = 18·t with t odd (since n is a multiple of 18 but not of 36).

We need the smallest n > 200 of the form 18·t with t odd. Solve 18·t > 200:
- 200/18 ≈ 11.11, so the smallest odd t > 11.11 is t = 13.

Therefore n = 18·13 = 234. Check: gcd(234, 36) = 18.

Answer: \boxed{234}

cmath_11685.pseudocode:
We look for the smallest two-digit prime p that can be written as a^3 + b^3 + c^3 with a,b,c positive integers.

Since p is two-digit (p < 100) and the cubes are positive, any cube term in the sum must be at most p. For the smallest two-digit primes (11, 13, 17, ...), we have p < 27, so any cube in the sum must be either 1^3 = 1 or 2^3 = 8 (because 3^3 = 27 would already exceed p).

- For p = 11: the only possible cube values ≤ 11 are 1 and 8. The sums of three numbers each in {1, 8} are:
  1+1+1 = 3, 1+1+8 = 10, 1+8+8 = 17, 8+8+8 = 24.
  None equals 11, so 11 is not expressible as such a sum.

- For p = 13: the same possible sums 3, 10, 17, 24 do not include 13. So 13 is not expressible.

- For p = 17: we can take 1^3 + 2^3 + 2^3 = 1 + 8 + 8 = 17. All terms are positive cubes, so 17 is expressible.

Thus the smallest two-digit prime that is the sum of three positive cubes is 17.

Answer: \boxed{17}

cmath_11738.pseudocode:

Therefore, the 1000th positive integer with an odd number of digits is

Let N = 20! = 1·2·3·...·20. The prime factors of 20! are exactly the primes ≤ 20, namely 2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13, 17, and 19.

A positive integer m > 1 is relatively prime to 20! if and only if m shares no prime factor with 20!. By the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic, this means m cannot have any prime factor ≤ 20. Therefore, all prime factors of m must be > 20, and the smallest such m is the smallest prime > 20.

The smallest prime greater than 20 is 23. Check: gcd(23, 20!) = 1 since 23 does not divide 20!.

Thus, the smallest positive integer > 1 that is relatively prime to the product of the first 20 positive integers is
\boxed{23}.

cmath_11870.pseudocode:
Model the situation as a simple graph with 22 vertices (one per person) and an edge between two vertices if those two people shake hands. Let E be the number of handshakes and let deg(v) be the degree of vertex v (the number of handshakes involving that person).

- Each person shakes hands with at most 20 others, so deg(v) ≤ 20 for all v.
- By the Handshake Lemma, the sum of degrees S equals 2E: S = ∑ deg(v) = 2E.
- Since there are 22 vertices, S ≤ 22 × 20 = 440, hence 2E ≤ 440 and E ≤ 220.

Achievability: Can we attain E = 220? Yes. Take the complete graph K22 (everyone shakes everyone: 231 edges), and remove a perfect matching (11 disjoint pairs of vertices) — this deletes 11 edges. The resulting graph has each vertex missing exactly one neighbor, so deg(v) = 20 for all v, and the total number of edges is 231 − 11 = 220.

Therefore, the maximum possible number of handshakes is boxed as:
\boxed{220}

3) Since 1/x + 1/y = 1/12 with positive x,y, we must have x > 12 and y > 12, so x − 12 and y − 12 are positive integers. Let a = x − 12 and b = y − 12. Then a, b are positive integers with ab = 144, and x ≠ y implies a ≠ b.

4) To minimize x + y = (a + 12) + (b + 12) = a + b + 24, minimize a + b under ab = 144 with a ≠ b. Check factor pairs of 144:
- (1,144) → sum 145
- (2,72) → 74

- (4,36) → 40
- (6,24) → 30
- (8,18) → 26

- (12,12) → 24 (but excluded since a = b)

The smallest valid sum is a + b = 25 with (a, b) = (9, 16) or (16, 9).

5) Then x = a + 12, y = b + 12. So (x, y) = (21, 28) or (28, 21), giving x + y = 49.

Answer: \boxed{49}

We rewrite the quadratic by completing the square.

x^2 + b x + 1/3
= (x + b/2)^2 - (b/2)^2 + 1/3

cmath_1291.pseudocode:

Let k = b − 6. Then b = k + 6 and
a = (373 − 5(k + 6))/k = (343 − 5k)/k = 343/k − 5.

For a to be a positive integer, k must be a divisor of 343 = 7^3. Thus
k ∈ {±1, ±7, ±49, ±343}, with b = k + 6 > 0 and a > 0.

Check the possibilities:

- k = 7: b = 13, a = 343/7 − 5 = 49 − 5 = 44. |a − b| = 31.

a, ar, ar^2 = a, b, c.

b^2 = a c.

We want the largest 3-digit number 100a + 10b + c with digits distinct, a ∈ {1,…,9}, b,c ∈ {0,…,9}, and b^2 = ac.

To maximize the number, start with the largest a, namely a = 9.

Then b^2 = 9c, so c must be chosen so that 9c is a perfect square. Write 9c = (3)^2 c; this is a square iff c is a perfect square. The possible c (digits) are 0, 1, 4, 9.

- c = 0: b^2 = 0 → b = 0, but digits are not distinct (9,0,0). Reject.
- c = 1: b^2 = 9 → b = 3. Digits (9, 3, 1) are distinct → 931 is valid.
- c = 4: b^2 = 36 → b = 6. Digits (9, 6, 4) are distinct → 964 is valid.
- c = 9: b^2 = 81 → b = 9, which duplicates a. Reject.

The valid numbers with a = 9 are 931 and 964. The larger is 964.

Therefore, the largest three-digit integer whose digits are distinct and form a geometric sequence is
\boxed{964}.

cmath_1779.pseudocode:
We have five vertices A,B,C,D,E and seven undirected edges: AB, AD, AE, BC, BD, CD, DE.

First note the degrees:
- deg(A)=3 (edges AB, AD, AE)
- deg(B)=3 (AB, BC, BD)
- deg(C)=2 (BC, CD)
- deg(D)=4 (AD, BD, CD, DE)
- deg(E)=2 (AE, DE)

Thus A and B are the only vertices of odd degree, so there exists an Euler trail (a route using every edge exactly once) that starts at A and ends at B. We count such trails by branching on the first edge from A.

Case 1: Start with AB.
- Now at B. Remaining edges: AD, AE, BC, BD, CD, DE.
- From B the next edge must be BC or BD.

Case 1.1: B → C (edge BC). Then at C only CD is possible, so C → D (edge CD). Now at D with remaining AD, AE, BD, DE.

- Case 1.1.1: D → A (AD). At A only AE remains, so A → E (AE). At E, only DE remains, so E → D (DE). At D only BD remains, so D → B (BD). This yields a valid trail:
  AB, BC, CD, AD, AE, DE, BD.

- Case 1.1.2: D → B (BD). Then at B there are no unused edges, so this path fails.

- Case 1.1.3: D → E (DE). At E only AE remains, so E → A (AE). At A only AD remains, so A → D (AD). At D only BD remains, so D → B (BD). This yields a valid trail:
  AB, BC, CD, DE, AE, AD, BD.

Case 1.2: B → D (edge BD). At D with remaining AD, CD, DE.

- Case 1.2.1: D → A (AD). Then A → E (AE). At E, DE remains, so E → D (DE). At D, CD remains, so D → C (CD). At C, BC remains, so C → B (BC). Trail:
  AB, BD, AD, AE, DE, CD, BC.

- Case 1.2.2: D → C (CD). Then C → B (BC). At B, remaining AD, AE, DE; but B has no unused edges, so invalid.

- Case 1.2.3: D → E (DE). Then E → A (AE). Then A → D (AD). Then D → C (CD). Then C → B (BC). Trail:
  AB, BD, DE, AE, AD, CD, BC.

Thus Case 1 yields 4 valid trails.

Case 2: Start with AD.
- Now at D. Remaining AB, AE, BC, BD, CD, DE. From D, choices are BD, CD, DE.

Case 2.1: D → B (BD). At B, choices AB or BC.

- Case 2.1.1: B → A (AB). Then A → E (AE). E → D (DE). D → C (CD). C → B (BC). Trail:
  AD, BD, AB, AE, DE, CD, BC.

- Case 2.1.2: B → C (BC). Then C → D (CD). Then D → E (DE). E → A (AE). A → B (AB). Trail:
  AD, BD, BC, CD, DE, AE, AB.

Case 2.2: D → C (CD). Then C → B (BC). At B, choices AB or BD.

- Case 2.2.1: B → A (AB). Then A → E (AE). E → D (DE). D → B (BD). Trail:
  AD, CD, BC, AB, AE, DE, BD.

- Case 2.2.2: B → D (BD). Then D → E (DE). E → A (AE). A → B (AB). Trail:
  AD, CD, BC, BD, DE, AE, AB.

Case 2.3: D → E (DE). Then E → A (AE). A → B (AB). Now at B with remaining AD, BC, CD, BD.

- Case 2.3.1: B → C (BC). Then C → D (CD). D → B (BD). Trail:
  AD, DE, AE, AB, BC, CD, BD.

- Case 2.3.2: B → D (BD). Then D → C (CD). C → B (BC). Trail:
  AD, DE, AE, AB, BD, CD, BC.

Case 2 yields 6 valid trails.

Case 3: Start with AE.
- Now at E. Only DE is available, so E → D (DE). From D, choices are AD, BD, CD.

Case 3.1: D → A (AD). Then A → B (AB). From B, choices BC or BD.

- Case 3.1.1: B → C (BC). Then C → D (CD). D → B (BD). Trail:
  AE, DE, AD, AB, BC, CD, BD.

- Case 3.1.2: B → D (BD). Then D → C (CD). C → B (BC). Trail:
  AE, DE, AD, AB, BD, CD, BC.

Case 3.2: D → B (BD). Then B → A (AB) or B → C (BC).

- Case 3.2.1: B → A (AB). A → D (AD). D → C (CD). C → B (BC). Trail:
  AE, DE, BD, AB, AD, CD, BC.

- Case 3.2.2: B → C (BC). Then C → D (CD). D → A (AD). A → B (AB). Trail:
  AE, DE, BD, BC, CD, AD, AB.

Case 3.3: D → C (CD). Then C → B (BC). From B, choices AB or BD.

- Case 3.3.1: B → A (AB). Then A → D (AD). D → B (BD). Trail:
  AE, DE, CD, BC, AB, AD, BD.

- Case 3.3.2: B → D (BD). Then D → A (AD). A → B (AB). Trail:
  AE, DE, CD, BC, BD, AD, AB.

Case 3 yields 6 valid trails.

Total number of Euler trails from A to B using every edge exactly once:
4 (Case 1) + 6 (Case 2) + 6 (Case 3) = 16.

Therefore, the number of different routes is:
\boxed{16}

3) yx - 2x = -1 - 5y
4) x(y - 2) = -(1 + 5y)
5) x = -(1 + 5y)/(y - 2) = (5y + 1)/(2 - y)

Thus f^{-1}(y) = (5y + 1)/(2 - y). Replacing y with x gives f^{-1}(x) = (5x + 1)/(2 - x). This corresponds to a = 5, b = 1, c = -1, d = 2, so
